Issued at 301 PM EDT Fri Oct 9 2026

===== This Afternoon through Tonight ====

Warm and dry conditions will continue this afternoon and evening, 
with temperatures topping out in the low-to-mid 80s. RH values are 
in the 20s in many areas, and this very dry air mass will take time 
to overcome as tropical moisture associated with Isaias starts to 
work its way into the region late tonight into Saturday morning. For 
this evening into tonight, light east winds and increasing cloud 
cover will keep temperatures milder, with lows Saturday morning only 
falling into the upper 50s and low-to-mid 60s.

===== Remnants of Isaias Move Through This Weekend =====

The main weather story from the Gulf Coast to the Ohio Valley this 
weekend will be Hurricane Isaias, which should make landfall in the 
FL panhandle this evening. Isaias is expected to lift fairly quickly 
to the north late tonight into Saturday before turning to the 
northeast and moving across the TN valley on Sunday. Deep moisture 
advection downshear from the TC center will overspread from south to 
north late tonight and through the day on Saturday. PW values are 
expected to rise from 0.6-0.7" this afternoon to over 1.50" by 
tomorrow evening, exceeding the 90th percentile of climatology. 
While the outermost bands of Isaias will likely end up as virga as 
the column saturates, rain should begin to reach the surface during 
the morning hours across southern KY, with the shield of rain likely 
becoming more broken/showery as it encounters the drier atmosphere. 
Scattered showers are expected to continue north, overspreading most 
of the area during the afternoon and evening hours.

Winds will increase through the day tomorrow as a 50 kt 850 mb jet 
moves into the region. While increasing saturation and cloud cover 
should limit momentum transfer later in the day, the strengthening 
pressure gradient should be sufficient for sustained easterly winds 
of 10-20 mph, with wind gusts of 25-35 mph likely. While there are 
low (10-40%) chances for occasional 40+ mph wind gusts, the expected 
coverage of such gusts should be low enough that a wind advisory is 
not needed. The strongest winds and gusts are expected from mid-
afternoon through a few hours after sunset, when increasing 
stability and weakening of the pressure/height gradient associated 
with Isaias will support easing winds. 

During the evening hours on Saturday into Saturday night, hi-res 
guidance suggests that a few bands of heavier showers and a few 
thunderstorms should set up across the eastern half of the CWA 
thanks to convergence along the leading edge of the LLJ as well as a 
plume of a few hundred joules of MUCAPE moving into the area from 
the southeast. In these bands, heavier rainfall totals would be 
expected, with 12Z REFS 6-hr LPMM amounts of 1-2" forecast east of I-
65. It should be noted that current 6-hr flash flood guidance is 3+" 
across the entire CWA, so these rainfall amounts would not be 
expected to cause flooding issues.

During the day on Sunday, the actual sfc low center is expected to 
pivot across southern KY and TN, with lingering low-level moisture 
supporting scattered showers and perhaps a few rumbles of thunder. 
Clearing should take place Sunday afternoon from west to east across 
the region as drier air wraps in. Overall, event total rainfall 
amounts have decreased since the previous forecast, with area totals 
generally on the order of 0.50-1". The highest rainfall amounts are 
now more likely along the I-75 corridor, where 24-hr LPMM amounts of 
1-2+" are more widespread. These rainfall amounts should ameliorate, 
but probably will not remove, ongoing drought conditions.

===== Next Week =====

After the remnant low pressure associated with Isaias clears the 
region to the east, upper level ridging and sfc high pressure is 
expected to set up over the south central and southeast US for the 
first half of the week. Fairly amplified troughing will set up in 
the intermountain west, with individual shortwaves riding up and 
over the ridge across the central CONUS through the first two-thirds 
of next week. Current medium-range guidance has a strong enough 
ridge over the region to keep most rain chances associated with the 
shortwave disturbances north of the area through Wednesday morning, 
though a low (20% chance) PoP will return for Wednesday and later 
into the week. Temperatures are expected to be unseasonably warm 
early next week as SW flow pushes highs into the low-to-mid 80s.

For Wednesday into the latter half of next week, the main forecast 
uncertainty centers around how the trough in the western CONUS 
evolves as it begins to eject to the east. There is relatively good 
agreement that an upper level wave and an associated cold front will 
push through the Ohio Valley, with spread in ensemble members on 
timing and strength of the system.
